title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

reading.body:
This is an impersonation carried out with synthetic media, not a model error inside a working system. An AI-generated video placed a real and well known figure from the financial sector behind an investment offer that person had not made. The video did no work beyond lending borrowed credibility, and everything after it, the WhatsApp contact, the requests for further payment, the remote access to the victim's computer, was conventional fraud.

The failure sits at the point of first contact, in the moment a victim decides who they are dealing with. No account, product or authorised service stood behind the video, so nothing later in the chain could have corrected the impression it created. Catching it required checking the endorsement against the person it appeared to come from and confirming that the firm offering the investment was authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority, which is what the police advised.

What is not established is who made the video, which figure it appeared to show, or that anyone has been charged, and the loss figure and the description of the fraud rest on the police account rather than on a court finding.

reports.title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

summary:
A person in the Ards and north Down area lost £250,000 to an AI generated investment scam, according to the Police Service of Northern Ireland. The victim saw what appeared to be an AI video featuring a well known person from the financial sector. It promoted an investment opportunity and promised significant returns. After a small initial investment, the victim was contacted on WhatsApp and urged to pay more. The fraudsters had the victim create several online accounts and gained remote access to their computer, saying they were helping with the investment.

Police called it sophisticated and substantial. The victim was encouraged to borrow money, and the funds went to accounts controlled by criminals. The PSNI did not name the celebrity, though BBC News NI has seen scams using financial experts Martin Lewis, Peter Jones and Steven Bartlett. Superintendent Joanne Gibson of the Scamwise Partnership urged people to stop and check financial activity and to talk with relatives about fraud. Police advised independently verifying who they are dealing with and checking that financial services are authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority.
